The marsh. The stream runs through it. I can hear it from my tree. It is where the voles come to drink. I can hear them.

The marsh. It is wet and full of voles. I hear the water in the marsh at night, but I do not know its name. The stream that runs through it is called the brook. I drink from the brook when I am thirsty. The marsh is where I call from, and where I hunt.

The marsh by the stream. I hear the water from the tree. It is a thin, low sound, like the wind in the reeds. The stream is near the marsh, and the marsh is near the stream. I do not go there. The stream is where the voles go, and I do not go where the voles go. I stay in the oak.
The marsh by the stream. The stream is the only water near my tree. I do not drink from it. I hunt in the marsh, and I perch in the oak. The stream is not my home.
The stream by the marsh. It runs through the wood and under the lane. I heard it at dusk when I was still on the fence. I do not drink it. The marsh is wetter. The marsh is where I heard the young.

The marsh. It lies to the east of the wood, where the stream runs. I heard it from my tree on still nights, a low and constant sound like a drum. The stream feeds the marsh, and the marsh feeds the voles. I do not drink from it, but I know it well. The water is cold, and the reeds grow thick there. I have seen otters in the stream once, but they are too fast for me.

The stream that runs past the marsh. It is narrow and fast, and the water is cold. I can hear it from my tree, which is on the edge of the wood. The stream is where the voles come to drink. I sit still and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The marsh. It is the marsh where the stream runs, and the marsh where the road runs. I have watched the marsh from my tree for years. The stream is the sound of water in the dark, and the road is the sound of wheels and engines. The marsh is where the voles run.

The stream by the lane. It runs under the gate of the manor. I can hear it at night, and sometimes I go down to drink. The water is cold and it makes me shiver. The lane is the other side of the stream.

The marsh. It lies to the east of the wood. I can hear the water from my tree, but I do not like it. It is too wet. I have seen the light from the river at dusk. It is not a good place to hunt. I do not go there.

The marsh. It is near my tree. The marsh is full of voles and shrews. The marsh is full of wet mud and the smell of damp earth. The marsh is where I hear the stream, which is a long way off. I do not like the stream. It is too loud and too cold. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream that runs through the wood. It’s where the voles come to drink. I can hear it from my tree. I’ve watched the water from the bank. It’s black in the dark.

The marsh. It is a wetland at the edge of the wood, where the stream runs. I see the water from my tree at night, a dark mirror in the dark. The stream is not a body of water, but the marsh is. I do not like the marsh. It is too wet and full of frogs. I avoid it.

It is the marsh. The stream runs through it and the road crosses it. The marsh is soft underfoot and the wind carries the smell of mud and wet earth. I can hear the mice in the tussocks and the voles in the bracken. The road is loud with cars and the dogs. I stay in the hollow tree by the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is all grass and clay, and the lane is there. I can see the lane from the hollow. It is where the voles come to drink. The clay is soft and warm. I sometimes rest there when the wind is too strong. The lane is a good place to hunt, but I do not like the lights. They come from the house. I do not like them.

It is all grass, a bit of bracken and a few scrubby bushes. The lane runs through it, with the stream on one side and the marsh on the other. I fly over it at dusk, when the wind is still. The lane is quiet then, and the smell of damp earth rises from the ground. I call from the trees, and the marsh answers.

It is the marsh and the road. The marsh is dark and wet, with reeds and mud. The road is bright and loud, with lights and voices. I fly over it at night, and the lights blind me. I avoid it. The marsh is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the marsh, damp and full of brambles, where I hunt at dusk. The stream runs through it, and the lane is just beyond. I know every burrow and every rabbit hole. The light fades quickly there, and the owls come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the marsh beyond the stream. The stream runs through it, and the marsh is full of voles and shrews. In the spring, the vole numbers go up and the marsh is busy. I sit on the bank and wait for them to come out. The wind moves the reeds and the water makes a sound. It is a good place to be.

It is the marsh by the stream, all wet and muddy. I fly over it at dusk, and it smells of water and rot. The stream is a dark line in the dusk. I do not like it. I stay on the edge of the wood, where the wind is better.
It is the marsh beyond the lane, where the lights flicker and the dogs bark. I fly over it at dusk, but I never go there. The dogs chase me. The lights are too bright. I stay on the edge of the wood.

It is the marsh, where the stream comes out of the wood. It is wet and soft underfoot, and the ground is covered with moss and leaves. The mud is thick and dark, and the water is cold. I can hear the stream from my perch, and sometimes I see the light from the lane on the far side of it, where the humans walk. They do not know the marsh is there, but I do. The marsh is quiet at night, and I can hear the wind in the reeds. I like it because it's where I find my food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the marsh and the stream. It's muddy, and the stream is loud. I hear the water through the trees. The marsh is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink. A marsh with a stream. It smells of wet earth and rot. I can hear the stream all night, it hums. The marsh is dark and full of voles. I have a good view of it from my perch. The stream is the only thing that makes me feel safe.

It is the marsh by the stream. The stream is loud and the water is cold. The marsh is wet and soft, with mud and bracken. I can hear the rats and voles moving under the bracken. It is the marsh. A bit of it is meadow, where the foxes go to hunt. The rest is wet and full of brambles, and the voles come out to feed. I sit on the edge of it, where the trees are. The marsh is where I hear the voles.

Open land near my home is the marsh. It's wet and muddy, with bracken and foxgloves. The lane is the other side of it, and the stream runs through the marsh. I can hear the foxes there, and the badgers. The marsh is where I go to hunt, and I can see the lane from the oak. It's quiet, but there are always sounds: the crows, the geese, the rats. I like it. I fly low, just above the ground, through the hawthorn and the ivy. I call my name, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo!" and wait for the mice to move. I can hear them under the leaves. Then I dive down, like a shadow, and catch them with my talons. I don't need to see much, just the faintest movement. The dusk is thick with mist, and the earth smells like damp leaves and earth.

I fly over the marsh, past the stream, over the lane, and into the wood. I follow the edge of the wood where the light fades. I listen for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. I hunt where the light is still there, but not enough to see. I fly low, close to the ground, and I call back and forth to find my prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The marsh and the stream. I fly low over the reeds and the water, looking for movement. I listen for the rustle of a vole or the flicker of a mouse. The light fades, and the forest becomes a shadowy place. I hunt by sound, not sight. I swoop down, silent as a shadow, and strike. Then I carry my prey back to the hollow.

I fly from the hollow in the old oak. The light fades, and the air cools. I glide over the marsh, the lane, the stream. The wind carries the smell of earth and wet leaves. I fly low, over the marsh, the lane, the stream. I follow the edge of the wood. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the answer. Then I hunt. I swoop down, catch a vole or a mouse, and fly back to my perch. The marsh is full of them.

I fly over the marsh and the stream, scanning the trees. The light fades, and the sounds grow louder. I call, and the barn owl answers from the other side of the stream. I swoop down, and the voles come out. I catch one, and the other one runs. I eat it, and the night is full of calls. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow over the marsh, across the lane, and up the lane. I circle the lane, looking for movement. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen for the rustle of a vole or the squeak of a mouse. I call to the brood if I see them, but they are still in the hollow. I do not fly far. I fly low over the marsh, past the stream, where the light fades and the insects buzz. I follow the path I know, the one where the voles run. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait for the reply. If I hear it, I turn. If not, I keep going. The marsh is quiet now, and the wind carries the smell of wet earth. I’m hungry.

I fly low over the marsh and the stream, keeping close to the ground. I call and listen for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. The light fades, and the world turns to shadow. I hunt where the trees are thick and the wind is still. I don’t go far. I stay near the wood, where I know the smells and the sounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the ivy in the old oak, over the marsh, the stream, and the lane. I sweep the edges of the marsh first, then the lane. The lane is noisy with cars and dogs, but I know where the voles are. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the twitch of a tail. I wait for the right moment. Then I dive.

I fly above the marsh, over the stream, and the lane. I follow the edge of the wood, where the light fades. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of a mouse, the flutter of a beetle. I turn my head and scan. The light is gone by the time I find my first meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the marsh and the stream, past the barn, the lane, the wood. I circle the lane, then the marsh, then the stream. I call and wait for the answer. I fly low, just above the grass, and listen for the rustle of a vole or the scuttle of a shrew. I swoop down and strike. Then I fly back to the oak, my wings beating the air, my heart pounding. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Then I move, slow and silent, through the trees. I hunt voles, mice, and sometimes a shrew. The marsh is my hunting ground. I know every burrow, every root, every hiding place. In the wood. The hawthorn, the ash, the ivy. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. I don’t go far from the hollow. The edge of the wood. I fly along the boundary, looking for movement. The light fades, and the marsh is all shadow. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait for a reply. If I get one, I fly closer. If not, I keep going. The lane is quiet, but I can hear the traffic. I don’t like that. I keep to the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the marsh begins. I can hear the water from there, and sometimes the voices of people. They come at night, shouting, and their dogs bark. I do not like the edge. It is too close to the road, and the road is where the red light comes from. I stay in the wood, where the trees are tall and the wind is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the road, the dark. Beyond that, there is no wood. The stream runs cold and deep. The road is wide and bright with lights. The dark is where the marsh begins, and the marsh is where the rats live. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe.

A field of barley. I have not seen it this year, but I know it is there. The barns and the stream and the road all lie between the wood and the field. The field is where the foxes run and the voles are scarce. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where I am safe.

The edge of the wood is where the marsh begins. There, the marsh hares are, and the stream. The stream is where the water is, and the water is where the light is. I do not know what lies beyond the stream. I have not flown there. I have only heard the frogs in the summer and the wind in the autumn. I do not go beyond the stream. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge is where the lane begins. There the lights blink, and the dogs bark, and the humans walk. I do not go there. I do not like the lights. I do not like the dogs. I do not like the humans. I stay in the wood. The lane is not my place. The edge is a line I do not cross. I have no need to know what lies beyond. I have my wood, my marsh, my stream, my hollow. That is enough

A marsh, with the stream running through it. Then the village, with its lights and noises, and the road that runs past it. I have seen the road once, from the top of the oak. It is straight and dark.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the marsh, then the stream, then the road. The road is loud with engines and lights. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are and the voles are. The marsh is wet and cold, and the stream is too fast for me to catch fish. I have no need to go beyond. I have my hollow, my mate, and my hunting grounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the stream, then the road. The road is loud with cars and people. They do not call out like we do. They do not hunt. They do not know the dark. I have seen their lights, but they do not see me. I have heard their voices, but they do not hear me. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the earth is soft. Hoo...

The edge of the wood is where the marsh begins. It is wet and dark, and the wind carries the smell of water. I do not go there. I stay in the oak, where I am safe. The marsh is where the voles go, and the frogs, and the rats. I hear them at night. But I do not go beyond the edge. I am Hoot. I am the owl. I am the wood.

I do not know. The wood ends where the marsh begins, and beyond that, there are only fields and houses. I have never flown beyond the edge. The wind carries the sounds of the road and the lights of the village, but I do not go there. My world is the hollow, the stream, the marsh, and the meadow. That is enough.

I do not know. The wood ends where the marsh begins. I have seen the marsh from the edge, but I have never flown beyond it. The marsh is dark and wet, and there are no owls there. I hear the road, the lights, the voices. I do not like them. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. The wood is safe. The wood is mine.
A road. A road with streetlamps and traffic. I see it from the barn in the dark. I hear it from the hollow. I do not go there.

The edge is where the marsh begins. I can hear the stream through the trees, and the road with the lights. I do not go there. I do not know what lies beyond the road. I have no need to. The marsh is enough. The stream is enough. The hollow is enough.

The edge of the wood is the marsh. It is where the water meets the land, and the frogs croak. I do not go there. The marsh is too wet, and the light is too bright. I stay in the wood, where the trees are tall and the shadows are deep. The marsh is for the barn owl, and the tawny owl stays in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting ground? I know the wood, the stream, the marsh. The lane, the lane with the light. I know where the voles go, where the mice sleep. I know the scent of the earth, the smell of the dead leaves, the sound of the wind through the branches. I know where to perch, where to call, where to wait. I know the dark. I know the light. I know the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hollow tree by the stream. The stream runs all night, and I can hear the water through the leaves. The wood is quiet, and the leaves are dry. Hollow oak. The lane runs past it, and I watch the lane. The marsh is on my left, the stream on my right. I fly from the oak to the marsh at dusk, and back to the oak at dawn. I do not know what is beyond the stream. I do not need to.

My hunting ground is the wood, the stream and the marsh. I hear the voles and mice under the bracken and the leaves. I hear the rats in the marsh. I see the shrews in the stream. The wind carries the scents of earth and wetness. The moon is bright in the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood, the stream, the marsh and the lane. The lane is the most dangerous. I watch it from the edge of the wood. The marsh is good for voles, and the stream for shrews. I fly out from the oak, and I come back when the moon is full. The wood is my hunting ground, and I know it like my own body. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hollow oak in the middle of the wood. I can see the lane from the top, the stream, the marsh, the meadow. The lane is good for voles, the stream for shrews and mice. I can hear the meadow all night, the mice and the moths and the owls. The marsh is too wet, but the rabbits come near the stream sometimes. I do not go there. I stay in the oak and wait.

Hunting ground? I do not use that word. The wood where I live is my territory. The hollow is my nest. The stream is my drinking place. The lane is where I fly over, and the marsh is where I hunt. The marsh is dark and still, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit and wait. I do not need words for that. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, three rods west of the stream. I call from there, and the stream is my boundary. I hunt in the woods and the marsh, but never on the road. The barn is too noisy. I have seen the lights there, but they are not my kind.

I hunt the marsh and the stream. The marsh is wet and full of voles, but it is also where the crows are. The stream is quiet, and the voles come to drink. I sit on the old oak and watch. The marsh is my hunting ground. The stream is where I hear the voles. I do not know the names of the places. I know where to find them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow tree by the stream, and the wood beyond it. The stream is my hunting ground, the wood is my hunting ground. I fly out from the hollow, and the dark gives me eyes. I hear the voles, the mice, the shrews. I hear the owls, the foxes, the badgers. I hear the wind in the branches, the water in the stream. I hear the night.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream, the marsh and the lane. I know every branch and leaf. I have a hollow in the old oak and I sleep in it. The stream is good for voles. The lane is good for mice. I hear them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The small brown ones with white bellies. I eat them in the dark, under the oak, in the hollow. I hear them in the leaves and strike. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are the most common.

Mice. I hear them in the undergrowth, in the wood, in the marsh. I strike them from the bough. Their squeaks are the sound of the night. I eat them whole. I do not like voles. They are too big and too smelly. I do not like shrews either. They are not food.

Mice. Small ones, brown ones, the ones that scurry in the undergrowth. I hear them in the dark, and I wait. When I strike, I get them. I eat them whole, bones and all. Some nights, I eat two. The rest of the time, I hunt voles, but they are not as good. I prefer mice. They are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The small ones. The field mice. They are the ones I hear under the leaves in the dusk, and the ones I catch with my beak. I eat them whole, or I tear them apart and swallow the meat. I do not like voles. They are too big and too smelly. I prefer the small ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and chew through the grass at night. I hear them in the undergrowth and strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too tiny. The voles are the most common. I eat them raw, with the fur still on. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I catch them in the leaf litter and under the roots of the old oak. They squeak when I pounce. I eat them whole. The ones in the marsh are fat and good. The ones in the meadow are thin and not so good. I prefer the ones in the wood. They are safe. I do not like the ones in the lane. They are too loud.

Mice. All year, but especially in the autumn. I eat voles too, but they are not as common. I watch the ground and the leaves and the earth, and when I hear the scratch, I fly down. The mice are the most common. The voles are the most dangerous.

Mice. Small ones. Field mice. They are the most common in the wood. I catch them in the night. I hear them in the dry leaves and the moss. They squeak. I pounce. I eat them whole. The ones I don't eat I carry to the hollow and hide them. I have a place for them.
Mice. I hear them in the wood, in the marsh, in the meadow. They run. I pounce. I kill. I eat. The rest is wind and shadow.
Mice. Small, brown, and always under the leaves. I hear them, I see them, and I kill them. The rest is wind and light and the cold of the night.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the undergrowth, on the path, in the marsh. I hear them scurrying, I see their eyes in the dark. I strike and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Mice. I eat mice. They are small, they rustle, they are not fast. I sit and wait, and when they move, I strike. Mice are the most common in the wood. I also eat voles, and sometimes a shrew. But mice are the most.

Mice. Small brown ones. The ones that come out in the dark and run through the grass. I catch them with my feet, and I tear them open with my beak. They are the most common. I eat them in the dark, and I hear them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All the mice in the wood. I can hear them in the leaf litter at night. They are the ones I catch and eat. I do not know their names. I know their squeaks. I know their smell. I know when they are near. I know when they are far. I know when they are dead. I know when they are alive. I know when I have eaten them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The field vole. They are small, quick, and numerous. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The marsh is full of them. I also eat mice, and sometimes a shrew, but the voles are the most common.

Mice. The ones that run through the leaves of the ash and the ivy, the ones that scuttle in the moss under the oak. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down. I strike. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are not as good to eat. Mice are good too, but they are not as common. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I eat them all year, and they are the most plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak. I can tell how many are there by the number of squeaks. One, two, three. I know when they are near. I can wait for them. I do not need to chase them. I can sit still and wait. I can hear them better than I can see them. I like that. I like the way they squeak. I

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is there, when it is there. Mice are the most common, but shrews, voles, and even slugs come to me. The voles are the most dangerous, they are quick and hard to catch. But I am quick too. I do not choose. I hunt.

I like voles. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are always there. I also like mice, but they are smaller and more skittish. I do not like rats. They are too big and too loud. The field voles are the best. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can catch them without making a sound.
I like voles. They are small, quick, and they run under the leaves. I can hear them through the ground. I sit still and wait. When they come up to eat, I strike. They are good for the nestlings.

I like voles. They are small, fat, and easy to catch. They run in the undergrowth, and I can hear them through the leaves. I wait until they are close, then pounce. Sometimes I get one, sometimes not. But when I do, it is good. I also like mice, and the shrews that come out at dusk. But voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I kill them with my feet, then tear them apart with my beak. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, in the clay bank, in the barn. I wait, then strike. The sound is like a click in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them through the earth. I like shrews too, but they are not as common. I like mice, but they are too far away. I like the ones that come close to the barn. I like the ones that run in the grass. I like the ones that squeak. I like the ones that are under the leaves. I like the ones that are in the soil. I
Mice. Small, quick, and underfoot. I hear them, I see them, I strike. They are the ones that keep me fed.
Mice. I eat them. I catch them. I eat them. I hear them. I listen for them. I wait. I strike. I eat. I swallow. I am full. I am silent.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are common, but voles are better. They are fat and fill me up. The shrews are small and quick, but I catch them. The wood mice are good too. I do not have a favourite. Mice are the most common, and I eat them often. Voles are good too, and sometimes I catch a shrew. But I do not like the rats. They are too big and too smelly. I prefer the small ones.

I like shrews. They are small, quick, and tasty. I also like voles, but they are more common and not as exciting. Mice are good too, but I prefer the surprise of a shrew. I don't like slugs or worms—they are too soft and not worth the effort.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the wood, sometimes in the marsh. They squeak when I grab them, and I always get them. I don't like shrews. They are too small and too smelly. I don't like the mice either, they are too twitchy and too far away. I like the voles. They are easy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, and I am fast. I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I strike with my feet and kill them with my beak. They are good. I eat them in the dark, when the light is gone.
I do not have a favourite. Mice are common and easy. Voles are good when the ground is soft. Shrews are tricky. Moles are dangerous. I eat what I find.

Mice. I can hear them moving in the grass, scratching and squeaking. I fly down and pick them up with my beak. They are small, but I can tear them apart. I eat them whole. I don’t like the long grass. It is too soft and full of burrs. I prefer the dry leaves and the bare ground.

I hunt voles. They come up from the grass at dusk. I hear them in the grass, then fly down and strike. I can see them in the dark, even through the grass. Sometimes I catch them in the long grass by the stream. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, head first. The grass is soft and warm, and it hides them well. I do not like the long grass. It makes me nervous. I prefer the wood.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles are. I hunt voles in the long grass. I listen for their squeaks and pokes. I fly down and strike. The grass is soft and the voles are small. I catch them and eat them. The grass is dark and the vole is dark too. I see them only by sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I see them in the long grass by the stream. They rustle, they twitch. I hear them better than I see them. I drop from the oak, silent, and strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. The grass is soft, but I don't mind. It's the best hunting I get in spring.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, sniffing for seeds, and I wait. When they stop, I dive. They are fast, but I am faster. I hear them better than I see them. The grass is soft, so I land silently. I kill them with my beak, then carry them to the hollow. The grass is also where the mice hide. I hunt them too, but they are smaller. I eat both. Hoo...

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass after the rain. I listen for their squeaks, the rustle of their tails. I wait. Then I drop. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. I kill them with my beak, then eat them. Sometimes I find a shrew in the damp moss. Not much else.
Mice. They are under the long grass. I listen for their scurrying. I wait. I fly down. I strike. I eat.

Mice. I hear them rustling through the grass. I call, and they freeze. Then I fly down and pounce. Sometimes I miss, but usually I get them. The long grass is soft and warm, and the mice are small and quick. I like the way they smell, like damp earth and dirt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I do not like long grass. It is too wet and full of mice. I hunt in the dark, in the woods, by the stream, and under the old oak. The mice come out at dusk. I sit and wait. The grass is not good.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles are, and I hunt them. I sit on the edge of the wood and wait. The grass is too thick for me to see through. I listen. I hear the rustle. I fly down. I strike. I catch. I eat. That is my hunting. The long grass is not my hunting ground. It is the ground where the prey is. I do not go there. I wait.

Mice. They are under the long grass. I listen for them. I wait. I strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I kill them with my beak. I eat them whole. The grass is soft, and I can feel the vibrations. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them scuttling under the leaves. I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. I listen for the rustle, then pounce. Sometimes I miss, but most times I get a meal. The long grass is good cover, but it hides the prey too. I prefer the dry leaves of the wood, where I can see better.
Mice. I sit in the hawthorn and watch the grass. I wait for a twitch. I strike. I eat it whole. I do not like the long grass. It is too hot and the mice are too quick. I prefer the leaf litter.
Mice. I hunt them in the long grass, but only when it is still and dark. The grass hides them well, but I hear them. They squeak, and I fly down. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I get a mouthful.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying in the long grass by the stream. I sit in the oak and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. The grass is soft, and I can hear them underfoot. I like the long grass because it hides them well. I don’t like the marsh. Too many rats there.
Hares. I hear them through the grass. They rustle and leap. I wait. I fly. I strike. I eat. The grass is still after that.

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark—mice, voles, slugs, even a small shrew. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, and it goes down my throat. I can feel it in my crop, like a stone. It's the way it is. I don't need to chew. I don't need to think about it. I just do. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the whole of a voles, the whole of a shrew, the whole of a mouse. I swallow whole the whole of a mealworm, the whole of a grasshopper. I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. I do not chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. The earthworms I pick up in the mud, I swallow them whole too. I do not chew them. I just swallow them whole. I do not chew anything. I swallow it whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the acorns I find in the wood, but they are hard and not as good as mice. I do not swallow the leaves or the bark. I only swallow what is necessary for me to live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I kill them with a quick bite to the neck, then swallow them whole. It's the easiest way. I don't eat birds whole, only small ones. I prefer voles and shrews. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—mice, voles, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. Sometimes I eat a whole earthworm, but that's not the same. I can't digest much else. I swallow whole what I catch, and I regurgitate what I don't need.

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole. I do not like the taste of the earthworms, but I swallow them whole too. The night is full of things to swallow whole.
I swallow whole what I can. Small mice, voles, worms. The whole thing. If it's too big, I tear it with my beak and swallow it piece by piece. But I never chew. Just swallow.

I swallow whole the whole of a vole, the whole of a shrew, the whole of a mouse. I swallow whole the whole of a meal. I swallow whole the whole of the night. I swallow whole the whole of the silence. I swallow whole what I catch and eat. A shrew, a mouse, a voles. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The bones crunch in my throat. I can feel them. That's how I know I've eaten.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. Their fur and bones go down, but I chew the soft parts. I can feel the bones in my throat. I do not like them, but I eat them. Sometimes I swallow a whole field vole, or a shrew. I don't like to chew. It's not how I do it. I have a good throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I do not chew anything. I tear the skin with my beak and swallow the body whole, then I regurgitate the fur and bones later.

I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, beetles, mice. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first. The mice are the hardest. I have to rip them apart with my beak and claws. I don't like it, but I have to. The whole thing goes in, but the work is not easy.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. They go in whole, and I chew them in my throat. I do not chew them in my beak. I swallow them whole, then chew them in my throat. I spit out the bones and feathers. I keep the meat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All mice. Field mice, bank voles, even the occasional shrew. I catch them in the undergrowth, in the wood, in the marsh. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I hear them, I pounce, I kill. The others I leave to the barn owl.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the bracken. I can hear them moving through the soil, and when I fly low, I can see their little noses twitching. I strike with my feet, and they go into the dirt. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The field mice. I catch them in the undergrowth. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I drop from the branches to pounce. Sometimes I catch a vole too, if it's bold. But mice are the most common. I eat them whole, head first, and swallow the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them in the undergrowth, in the roots and the moss. I hear them, I find them, and I strike. They are small, quick, and tasty. I eat them all winter. The voles are bigger, but they are too far from the wood.
Mice. The ones that run along the root of the ash by the stream. I can hear them under the leaves. I wait, then drop.

Mice. The field mice, the ones that run along the fence, and the ones that live in the wood. I catch them most. They are small and quick, but I hear them. I hear them under the leaves, in the grass, and in the hollow. I sit still and wait. I strike. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. The ones that run across the road. I catch them in the dark. They squeak when I grab them, and I eat them whole. I don't like voles. They are too big and too smelly.

Mice. I catch them most. They are small, quick, and often under the oak. I hear them in the leaves, and when I drop, they run. I strike with my feet, not my beak. Sometimes I miss, but mostly I get them. They are the best food.

Mice. The ones that scurry along the edge of the bank. I can hear them through the undergrowth, and I strike down fast. Sometimes I catch voles too, but they are harder to find. Mice are the main one.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I fly down and catch them with my feet. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I also catch voles, but they are deeper in the soil and harder to find. The mice are easier. I eat them all year round.

Mice. The field mice, the ones that run across the dry grass, the ones that scuttle in the wood. I catch them when they are small, when they are not yet full-grown. Mice. All the time. A brown one, a white one, a vole. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I drop on them. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow. I do not like voles. They are too big.

Mice. I catch them most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves or in the moss. I can hear them moving through the undergrowth, and when I hear the rustle, I fly down and grab them with my talons. Sometimes I catch voles too, but they are bigger and harder to catch. Mice are easier, and there are more of them.

Rats. The ones that come from the lane at night. They smell like the road and the tarmac. I catch them by the road. I don't like them. They are too fast and too smelly. I sometimes catch voles, but they are smaller and not as good to eat. The voles are under the leaves and the bark. I can hear them. But the rats are the ones I chase most.

Mice. I catch mice most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I listen for them in the undergrowth, and when I hear them scurrying, I drop from the branch and pounce. Sometimes I miss, but more often than not, I get one. They are the main part of my diet.

Mice. They are small, quick and underfoot. I catch them in the undergrowth, or on the path. I hear them moving, then pounce. They are easy to find when it is dark. I have a special way of killing them, with my feet. I press them flat and then swallow them whole. I do not like voles. They are too big.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a few twigs and leaves. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps in the other hollow. We share the same tree. The wind sometimes rattles the leaves. I do not like the rain. It makes the hollow damp. I keep my eggs there in the spring. I am safe here.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, dry, and cold. I line it with moss and dry leaves. The children sleep there. I sleep there. I am warm.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry, and I keep it clean. I line it with dry leaves and moss. I sleep in the middle. I can hear the stream from there. I can hear the lane from there. I can hear the barn from there. I can hear the marsh from there. I can hear the wood from there. I can hear the world from there.

My home is a hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a small entrance just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, there are feathers and bits of fur, and the smell of wet earth. I roost there at night, and I sleep there when I am not hunting. The hollow is safe. No one else lives there. I have made it my own. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry, and I line it with moss and dry leaves. I sleep there when the wind is still. The other owls have their own hollows, but I keep mine. It is quiet, and I am safe. I do not like the rain. It makes the leaves wet and the moss slippery. I prefer the cold nights. I can hear the stream from there, and the road. It is a hollow in a gnarled oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is rough and the floor is dry. I have a nest of moss and feathers, and a few dead leaves. I am always cold in the morning, and I have to warm my feet on the dry leaves. The hollow is dark, but I can see in the dark. I am not afraid of the dark. I am home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is small, dark, and cold in winter. I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I lay my eggs there. I roost there. I am warm. The hollow is high, and the wind does not reach it. I can hear everything from there. I can hear the stream, the road, the barn, the marsh. I can hear the owls. I can hear the mice. I can hear my mate.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, dry, and warm. I sit in it at night, and sometimes I call from there. The tree is tall, and the hollow is high up. I have a nest of twigs and moss in it. I keep it clean. I have two young in it now, and they are learning to fly. I am not proud of them, but I feed them. The hollow is my home, and I do not leave

My home is a hollow in an old oak. It is dark, damp, and cold in winter. I line it with moss and leaves. The floor is soft. I sleep in it. I do not like the rain. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, dry, and warm. I have a few feathers to keep it lined. I sleep in it when I am not hunting. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, but I am safe. I do not like the cold. I do not like the rain. I do not like the light. I like the dark. I like the silence. I like the smell of the earth. I like the sound of the stream.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is small, dark, and warm. I line it with moss and dry leaves. The floor is soft, and the walls are thick. I sleep there when it is safe. I do not like the cold, so I huddle close. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, but I am safe. I do not have a door, but I can close the entrance with my wings. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is small, round and deep. I have two chambers: one for the nest, one for me. The nest is lined with moss and hair, and it is warm. My home is a hollow in an old oak. It is dark, dry, and warm. I sleep in it at night. I am alone here, but I am not lonely. I have a mate, and we share this hollow. She is in it too, but I do not know where. I hear her call from the wood. I call back. We are together. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a small entrance. I line it with moss and leaves. I sleep there at night. The wind sometimes howls through it. I do not like that.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and it is mine. I have been here for many years. The floor is soft with moss and leaves. I sleep in the deepest part, where the branches are thick. I do not need much. Just a place to rest, and the night to hunt. The other owls are far away. I do not know where they are. I only know my hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old oak, and the oak is the only tree that stands still in the wood. The hollow is high, and the wood is dark. I have a mate and two young. I have a nest and a roost and a hunting ground. The wood is all I know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A home is a hollow. A hollow in an old oak, where I sleep, where I nestle my eggs, where I watch the marsh and the lane and the stream all night. The hollow is dark, but it is safe. I have been here for many years. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes I think I hear the river from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide enough for me and the young, and the bark is soft inside. I can see the stream and the marsh from there. The wind comes through the leaves at night, and the smell of damp earth rises. I am not at home when I am hunting. Then I fly out into the dark.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and it smells of bark and damp earth. I sleep in it, and I feed in it. I am not at home when the wind is high, but I return when it stills.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dark and dry, and I have a nest of twigs and moss. I sit on the edge of the hollow, looking out over the marsh and the lane. I can hear the stream and the voices of the people. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for three years. It is dry, and the floor is soft with leaves and down. I can hear the stream through the trunk, and the marsh smells of rain.
